depth.h2: What Geneva Homes Need From a Plumber
depth.intro: The median home in Geneva was built in 1987, but the oldest houses in its historic district go back to the 1840s. About 1 in 10 homes were built before 1940, and more than 4 in 10 went up after 1990. Each era brings its own plumbing problems.

tiles.title: Historic Homes Near the Fox River
tiles.body: The Central Geneva Historic District runs along the Fox River, and most of its houses were built between 1840 and 1900. Homes from that era often still have cast iron drains, galvanized water lines and clay sewer pipe. Galvanized pipe rusts from the inside and slowly cuts water pressure, and clay pipe cracks and lets roots in. A [camera inspection](/geneva/video-camera-sewer-inspections) shows the condition of your line before you decide on a [sewer repair](/geneva/sewer-repair).

tiles.title: Heavy Rain and Basement Backups
tiles.body: In September 2008, about 9 inches of rain fell on Geneva in two days, and basements flooded across much of Kane County. Heavy rain still tests every sump pump here. A [sump pump with a battery backup](/geneva/sump-pumps) keeps running when the power goes out, and a [backflow valve](/geneva/flood-control-maintenance) stops sewage from coming up through floor drains.

tiles.title: Newer Neighborhoods, Original Equipment
tiles.body: More than 4 in 10 Geneva homes went up after 1990. Equipment that came with the house, like the first water heater and the first sump pump, isn’t built to last 20 or 30 years. A [water heater that leaks or runs out too fast](/geneva/water-heater-repair) is usually the first to go. A [whole-home checkup](/geneva/plumbing-maintenance) tells you what’s close to the end before it fails.

tiles.title: Winter Freezes and Hidden Leaks
tiles.body: Fox Valley winters bring long stretches below freezing. Pipes in exterior walls, crawl spaces and outdoor spigot lines freeze first, and a split pipe often starts leaking inside a wall once it thaws. We can [find and fix the leak](/geneva/leak-repairs), and we’re on call 24/7 if a [pipe bursts](/geneva/burst-pipe-repair).

items.q: How much does a plumber cost in Geneva?
items.a: It depends on the job. The main factors are what’s wrong, how hard it is to reach, the parts or materials needed and the age of your plumbing. A historic home near the river with original cast iron and clay pipe can take more work than a newer one. We give you a flat-rate price before any work begins, so you know the cost going in. Give us a call and we’ll walk you through it.

items.q: My home in Geneva’s historic district is over 100 years old. What should I check?
items.preview: Start with the sewer line and the water lines.
items.a: Start with the sewer line and the water lines. Homes from that era often have clay sewer pipe, cast iron drains and galvanized water pipe, and all of them wear out with age. A camera inspection shows the condition of your sewer line, and low water pressure is often a sign that galvanized pipe is closing up inside. Age alone doesn’t mean something is wrong, but an inspection lets you plan repairs instead of reacting to a leak.

items.q: When should I replace my water heater?
items.preview: Tank water heaters usually last somewhere around 8 to 12 years.
items.a: Tank water heaters usually last somewhere around 8 to 12 years. Rusty water, rumbling noises, a leak at the base or hot water that runs out faster than it used to all mean it’s time to have it checked. [Replacing it](/geneva/water-heater-installation) on your schedule is easier than dealing with a flooded basement.

items.q: Can tree roots damage my sewer line?
items.preview: Yes. Roots grow toward moisture and slip into sewer lines through cracks and loose joints, especially in older clay pipe.
items.a: Yes. Roots grow toward moisture and slip into sewer lines through cracks and loose joints, especially in older clay pipe. Early signs include slow drains, gurgling and backups in the lowest drain in the house. A camera inspection shows whether roots are the cause, and [hydro jetting](/geneva/hydro-jetting) or a [sewer repair](/geneva/sewer-repair) can clear them out.

items.q: How do I protect my basement from sewer backups?
items.preview: Start with three things: a backflow valve on your sewer line, a sump pump with a battery backup, and a regular check of your sewer line for roots and debris.
items.a: Start with three things: a backflow valve on your sewer line, a sump pump with a battery backup, and a regular check of your sewer line for roots and debris. For homes with repeat backups, an [overhead sewer system](/geneva/overhead-sewer-systems) lifts basement wastewater above the level where backups happen. We can look at your setup and tell you which option makes sense for your home.
